web_title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Chapter 2: Inside the Machine Families — Turning, Milling, NEXA & Defence
question: What exact machines does Macpower build, how do its product families and end-markets split, and how does a customer actually use them on a factory floor?

epigraph.quote: A machine tool is the mother machine: every gear, valve, missile casing, and engine block begins its physical life on a spindle.
epigraph.author: Indian Machine Tool Industry Maxim

web_blocks.html: Macpower CNC Machines Limited operates as a single Ind-AS segment: CNC metal-cutting machine tools [2, 15]. At its 8-acre Metoda plant, it builds over 388 models and variants across six core machine types [4, 15]. These include Turning Centers, Vertical Machining Centers (VMCs), Horizontal Machining Centers (HMCs), Vertical Turret Lathes (VTLs), Double Column Machines (DCMs), and 4+1 / 5-axis units [4, 8, 15]. It also builds proprietary 'Macatrol' controllers and robotic or gantry automation cells [4, 15]. Because Macpower does not publish annual segment revenue splits, its FY23 audited mix serves as our baseline, while order-book data shows how fast the mix is upgrading [15, 18].

web_blocks.takeaway: While Turning Centers historically anchored ~64% of sales, average machine realization has climbed to ₹20.36 lakh in Q2 FY27 because NEXA large-format machines now represent 40% of the ₹476.7 Cr order book [4, 15].

web_blocks.html: To see why customers buy across these families, it helps to separate the physics of metal cutting. A CNC Turning Center spins a steel bar or forged blank at high RPM against a stationary cutting tool [15]. This setup works best for round parts like transmission shafts, wheel hubs, hydraulic fittings, and pump impellers [15]. Macpower's Turning Center line spans basic 2-axis lathes to twin-spindle units that cut two parts at once [15]. Newer Turn-Mill centers, like the TOM 200 launched in Q1 FY27, add a Y-axis milling head to drill off-center holes in a single clamping [15].

A Machining Center flips the physics. The workpiece stays clamped on a precision table while a fast-spinning tool moves across X, Y, and Z axes [15]. Vertical Machining Centers (VMCs) hold the spindle upright and serve die-and-mould shops, EV battery housings, and electronics casings [15]. Horizontal Machining Centers (HMCs) mount the spindle sideways with a rotary pallet changer [15]. That layout lets a factory machine four faces of a heavy casting—such as a tractor gearbox or armoured-vehicle engine block—in one setup [15].

At the top of Macpower's lineup sits the NEXA vertical, built to replace heavy imported machines [4, 15]. NEXA covers Vertical Turret Lathes (VTLs) for large rings and valve bodies, plus bridge-style Double Column Machines (DCMs) [15]. Examples include the 30-tonne DCM 4222 (priced near ₹2 Cr) and the 5-metre DCM 5227 launched in Q2 FY27 for railway bogies, aerospace tooling, and large moulds [15]. Macpower has also proven 5-axis capability and won a ₹2 Cr single 5-axis order, with a new aerospace/defence model slated for IMTEX January 2027 [6, 15]. Still, CMD Rupesh Mehta calls simultaneous 5-axis a niche 'Ferrari' market in India of only 150–200 units per year [6, 15]. It also faces heavy 300-page German BAFA export-control rules on Siemens controllers [6, 15].

web_blocks.title: Concrete Real-World Customer Examples (MSME Job Shop to T-90 Tank & Chandrayaan-3)
paragraphs: 1. Automotive Tier-2 Job Shop (Volume Core): A Pune or Rajkot supplier making shafts and EV motor housings for OEMs like Hero MotoCorp or Kirloskar buys a cluster of Turning Centers and Twin-Spindle VMCs (~₹20–25 lakh each). The buyer puts down a 10%–20% booking advance and takes an MSME bank loan, often backed by a state subsidy. Delivery follows bank disbursement, and the shop relies on a Macpower engineer within 24 hours if a spindle alarms [15].

2. Engine Factory Avadi & ISRO (High-Precision Proof Points): Macpower supplied a custom HMC to Engine Factory Avadi to machine parts for the T-90 Bhishma tank. It also delivered VMCs used by ISRO's vendor base for Chandrayaan-3 mission hardware [12, 15]. In May 2026, HAL (builder of the LCA Mk1A fighter) placed a ₹3 Cr custom order with a 6-month build cycle [15].

web_blocks.html: Customer concentration is very low. Macpower serves over 1,250 auto firms, 775 general engineering shops, 157 die-and-mould makers, 87 farm-equipment firms, 35 defence units, and 6 aerospace units [15]. No single buyer accounted for 10% or more of revenue in FY25 or FY26 [3, 15]. That spread protects Macpower from single-client cancellations, though MSME buyers still depend on bank credit and capex mood [15]. Meanwhile, an in-house team of 30+ engineers builds proprietary 'Macatrol' controllers, gantry loaders, and robotic cells for lights-out auto and electronics lines [15].

book_paragraphs: If you want to understand Macpower CNC without drowning in engineering jargon, picture two opposite ways of carving metal. In the first, you spin a block of steel like a potter's wheel and press a sharp blade against it to shave off rings and grooves. That is a Turning Center, and it is how you make round parts: automotive axles, hydraulic valves, pump shafts, and gear blanks. In FY23, the last year Macpower broke out its product mix, Turning Centers made up 64.3% of revenue, or ₹127.6 crore. It is the bread-and-butter cash engine of the company, sold by the hundreds to small and mid-sized auto-ancillary factories across Pune, Rajkot, Chennai, and the Delhi-NCR belt. From basic two-axis lathes to twin-spindle machines that cut two parts simultaneously, Turning Centers keep the Rajkot assembly lines humming year-round.

Now picture the opposite: you bolt a heavy, boxy casting onto a flat table so it cannot move, and you bring a spinning drill or milling cutter down from above—or in from the side—to carve pockets, holes, and contours. That is a Machining Center, which accounted for 34.9% of FY23 sales, or ₹69.3 crore. A Vertical Machining Center works from above and is the workhorse of die-and-mould shops, EV battery-housing fabricators, and consumer-electronics manufacturers. A Horizontal Machining Center works from the side with a rotating pallet changer, allowing it to machine four faces of a heavy engine block or tractor gearbox housing in a single clamping without an operator stopping the cycle.

Let me give you two concrete examples so you can see how these machines earn their keep in the real world. First, imagine a Tier-2 auto-parts vendor in Pune making transmission shafts and pump bodies for Hero MotoCorp or Kirloskar. That shop owner does not want an exotic ₹2 crore European machine; they want a reliable ₹20 to ₹25 lakh Macpower Turning Center or Turn-Mill machine—such as the newly launched TOM 200 with a Y-axis—financed through an MSME bank loan and often backed by a state capital subsidy. They pay a 10% to 20% booking deposit, take delivery when the bank releases the funds, and rely on a local Macpower service engineer to reach their shed within 24 hours if a spindle alarms.

Second, travel south to the Engine Factory Avadi, where India builds engines for the T-90 Bhishma main battle tank, or to ISRO's vendor ecosystem that machined precision hardware for the Chandrayaan-3 lunar mission. There, Macpower's Horizontal and Vertical Machining Centers are cutting aerospace alloys and armoured-vehicle engine housings to micron tolerances. Similarly, Hindustan Aeronautics Limited—the builder of the LCA Mk1A fighter jet—placed a ₹3 crore custom machine order in May 2026 with a six-month build cycle. While defence and aerospace still represent a single-digit share of total revenue today (roughly ₹20 crore of orders in hand in July 2026), those 200+ machines in 35 defence factories and 100+ machines in 6 aerospace units serve as priceless technical proof points.

That brings us to NEXA—the bridge between those two worlds. A few years ago, Macpower realized that while standard turning centers kept the factory busy at ₹15 to ₹20 lakh a machine, Indian railways, wind-energy firms, and heavy die-makers were importing massive double-column bridge machines and vertical turret lathes from Taiwan and Europe for ₹1 to ₹2 crore apiece. So Macpower built the NEXA line completely in-house—machines like the 30-tonne DCM 4222 and the 5-metre DCM 5227 launched in Q2 FY27. By September 2026, NEXA had grown to 40% of Macpower's ₹476.7 crore order book, quietly pulling the company's average machine realization up toward ₹20.36 lakh.

Yet notice the discipline in what management refuses to chase blindly. In July 2026, Rupesh Mehta called simultaneous 5-axis machines the 'Ferrari' of the CNC world—a niche of just 150 to 200 machines a year in India, bogged down by 300-page German BAFA export-compliance agreements on Siemens controls. Macpower built a 5-axis machine to prove its engineering capability and won a ₹2 crore order, but Mehta refuses to bet the company's scarce floor space on a compliance-heavy niche when the core import-substitution market in NEXA and standard CNCs is wide open. With over 1,250 auto customers, 775 engineering firms, and zero single customer above 10% of sales, Macpower's revenue base is remarkably well diversified.

book_callouts.title: THE RAZOR-AND-CATALOGUE REALITY
book_callouts.text: Unlike software, a CNC machine maker cannot sell one universal SKU. Macpower maintains 388+ models and variants because every auto part, valve, or tank housing demands a specific bed length, spindle torque, and chuck size. That breadth wins orders—but as we will see in Chapters 3 and 6, it also forces the company to carry 20,000+ part types in inventory.
